articles.title: Omar says raid was trying to ‘freak her out,’ 17 items including phones taken
articles.summary: Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) said the federal law enforcement raid on her home was an attempt to “freak all of us out,” revealing that agents took 17 items, including her phones. “Well, I mean, you don’t show up to somebody’s house that early in the morning unless you’re trying to freak them out,” Omar told MS…
articles.body:
Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) said the federal law enforcement raid on her home was an attempt to “freak all of us out,” revealing that agents took 17 items, including her phones.

“Well, I mean, you don’t show up to somebody’s house that early in the morning unless you’re trying to freak them out,” Omar told MS NOW’s Chris Hayes. “And, you know, it obviously did freak all of us out. I only had two and a half hours of sleep when they came, pounding on the doors.”

The lawmaker described how Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers “surrounded the house” at 6:00 a.m. before “pounding on the back door and the front door.”

“We were screaming. We were coming down. Our bedroom’s upstairs, trying to put on clothes and, you know, trying to run down before they broke the door,” she continued.

She said the agents provided her a search warrant before going “room by room” and seizing 17 items, including her phone and other electronics.

“They took my phone, an old phone, I believe, that was a travel phone of mine. My youngest daughter’s first phone was also old, sitting in her room. And then a phone that I’d just gotten replaced that was still in my possession,” she said.

“I was surprised when they handed me the receipt for the items that they’d taken to do that long of a search and to walk away with 17 items of like 10 that were just notebooks and like old phones was such a bizarre, bizarre thing.”

The raid drew attention , as Justice Department policy usually discourages the escalation of politically sensitive investigations within 60 days of elections. The Justice Department said in a statement the raid was “part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation.”

President Trump and his administration have claimed Omar’s father lied about her age when she obtained U.S. citizenship in 2000 after their family emigrated from Somalia.

The Democratic lawmaker has denied these allegations and accused the Trump administration of waging a “campaign of political intimidation” against her in a social media post following the raid.

articles.title: Kara Swisher predicts Democrats will try to jail Elon Musk
articles.summary: Another day, another series of warnings from Democratic and liberal media figures that they are going to try to put their political opponents in jail if they take back control of government.
articles.body:
Another day, another series of warnings from Democratic and liberal media figures that they are going to try to put their political opponents in jail if they take back control of government.

You heard this from Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin earlier this week — remember when she said she hoped all those forthcoming prosecutions of administration officials would scare away young Republicans and prevent them from getting involved in politics?

Well this time, it’s liberal commentator Kara Swisher, who says that Elon Musk better watch out. If Kamala Harris was president, he might be in jail — and if Democrats take back control of Congress, they will find a reason to get him.

Let’s watch her on “The Bulwark” podcast.

Call me old fashioned, but I don’t think it’s a good thing that everybody has to be completely invested in national politics in order to save their own skins, because losing means prison. This is America, and losing should mean, well, losing. Your guys are out, you wish the other team the best of luck, and you wait for your turn to get back into power. We are verging on having a system in which the losers face legal repercussions, and very serious ones, which means there is even more of an incentive to not lose. If the risks are existential, you’re gonna fight harder, or even dirty.

By the way, this is a common fate for political figures in other countries: Win or face prosecution. These are features of banana republics. It’s not what we want for our country.

Unfortunately, the Dems are giving every indication that they are going to prosecute their political enemies. The crime is TBD: They’ll figure it out later, but they’ll find something. Then they turn around and complain when the Trump administration investigates Ilhan Omar’s immigration status. But they’re perfectly OK predetermining that Musk should face jail time? Musk, the world’s most important tech founder, who builds rockets and flying cars, whose systems provide internet to Ukraine and defensive capabilities for their forces there, who is indispensable to the fate of the free world? Kamala Harris should have looked for a reason to jail him?

No wonders he’s become such a full-throated defender of Donald Trump. He has no choice.

This just isn’t how it’s supposed to be, and so I wish that the Democrats were capable of elevating more temperamentally moderate voices, of emphasizing that their concern is justice, not vengeance, and that they will ultimately put the country first, not the narrow interests of their party.

Can they do that? Can they say that? Or are they really going to try to jail all their enemies, come hell or high water? Frightening, and anti-American.

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.title: Dolly Parton’s sister says machine changed her vote to Republican
articles.summary: A number of voters, including Dolly Parton's sister, Stella Parton, have taken to social media to report problems with voting machines.
articles.body:
Voters in Middle Tennessee have flocked to social media just a week into early voting to report ballot issues at polling stations.

Over the past few days, a number of voters, including Dolly Parton 's sister, Stella Parton, have taken to social media to report problems with voting machines, saying the devices did not display their desired candidate or changed their selections.

The reported complications come after hundreds of thousands of Tennesseans started casting ballots on Oct. 14 for governor , U.S. Congress, the Tennessee General Assembly and three proposed constitutional amendments .

It's officially Dolly Parton Day! See celebrations for the late icon

Today is Dolly Parton Day! Across the country, countless counties, cities and even two states have declared Friday, Sept. 25, as Dolly Parton Day to honor the late "Queen of Country," who died at the age of 80 on Aug. 25. The day, 9-25, honors Parton's popular song "9 to 5." See celebrations honoring the late icon's legacy and life. People take photos with the Dolly Parton statue after Sevier County came together to proclaim Sept. 25 as Dolly Parton Day at the Sevier County Courthouse in Tennessee on Sept. 25, 2026.

Here's what voters are reporting and how election officials recommend verifying your ballot.

What exactly are Tennessee voters reporting on social media?

Social media users have reported needing multiple attempts to cast ballots for their preferred candidates because of alleged issues with electronic voting machines.

Stella Parton took to Facebook on Oct. 21 and encouraged voters to check their ballots after she said it took her three attempts to select her preferred candidate.

"Again, I remind you to double check your ballot before you print it out and put it through the machine," wrote Parton .

"I finally called over a poll worker when my ballot kept flipping to the wrong candidate on the third try. No, this is not a joke! But what good is your vote if the machines are 'fixed' this is the issue here."

"So, this happened to me when I early voted the other day… at the time I just attributed it to fat finger syndrome, but I have seen more and more people in Tennessee saying this has happened to them too," another Facebook user added.

Following her initial post, Parton shared a separate Facebook post , urging voters to hit the polls despite the issue.

"In Tennessee last week at the Hermitage Library where I voted, I had to go back three times and correct my vote because it kept defaulting to Marsha Blackburn. I would never vote for her for anything.

"I'm putting this out here because when we vote, we take it seriously but we try not to hold up the long lines. Do it anyway. Don't let them rig this election."

"There is a very disturbing trend being seen in early voting. Texas, Florida, Tennessee, Ohio are reporting difficulties getting the machines to accept democratic votes. The machines change them back to Republican unless the voter persists, pressing several times to get the correct vote to go through," an X user wrote.

How the Tennessee Secretary of State's office says voters should check their ballots

"Tennessee's voting systems are designed with multiple safeguards to help ensure that ballots are recorded consistent with voter intent," Tennessee Coordinator of Elections Mark Goins told The Tennessean regarding the reported issues.

In addition to assuring voters that Tennessee's voting system has multiple safeguards, Goins reminded voters of the several opportunities they have to verify their selections before casting a ballot, including the selection screen, review screen and paper record.

What to do if you encounter issues at the polls

If voters encounter problems at the polls like the ones mentioned, they should immediately notify a poll worker or their local county election commission so the issue can be addressed before the ballot is cast.

Tennessee election officials also encourage voters to carefully review their ballot selections before final submission. The Tennessee Secretary of State provides election resources and contact information on their website .

articles.title: Ted Cruz baselessly claims El-Sayed may share Intel with terrorists
articles.summary: I don’t hear Republicans saying the same thing to Catholic candidates, or Christian candidates — there are extremist organizations within both religions.
articles.body:
Texas Sen. Ted Cruz went on Fox News this week and suggested Dr. Abdul El-Sayed could endanger American lives by sharing classified information with terrorists, without any evidence for that extraordinary accusation. Why must Republicans continue to use a candidate’s religion as political weapon?

“Chuck Schumer could place Abdul El-Sayed on the Senate Intelligence Committee. He would have access to the very highest level of classified materials. And I believe, if that were to happen, there would be an unacceptably high risk that American servicemen and women, their lives would be endangered, and that our covert intelligence assets, their lives would be in danger because every reason to believe Abdul El-Sayed would share that classified information with Muslim Brotherhood terrorists.”

That’s a serious allegation. But El-Sayed denies having ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, and there is no established public evidence that he is a member of the organization. At all.

The Republican talking point is that El-Sayed signed a 2012 letter supporting Egyptian President Mohamed Morsi. Supporting Morsi in that letter is not the same as pledging allegiance to the Brotherhood. The goal of the open letter was to rid Egyptian leadership of any supporters of the dictatorship that had been toppled during the Arab Spring. At the time, El-Sayed and other pro-democracy advocates viewed Morsi’s election as a clean break from decades of military rule and a step toward self-determination for Egyptians.

Earlier this month at town hall, El-Sayed firmly rejected the Muslim Brotherhood and firmly stated to an audience member who asked about it: “You’re asking the question because, implicitly, you assume that I’ll have dual loyalties, right? You assume that I wouldn’t disavow, or that I’ll have some higher order allegiance than to the Constitution, correct?”

Meaning simply because he’s Muslim, he would put religious loyalty above his constitutional obligations. I don’t hear Republicans saying the same thing to Catholic candidates, or Christian candidates — there are extremist organizations within both religions.

Meanwhile, during their first debate, Republican Mike Rogers tried to draw a connection between El-Sayed’s mom and al Qaeda, and President Trump has even mocked El-Sayed’s name and started calling him by his middle name, Mohamed.

But all of these are not isolated incidents. Look at what Republican lawmakers have posted on social media this year alone:

Tennessee Congressman Andy Ogles posted on X in March that Muslims “don’t belong in American society.”

Also in March, Florida Congressman Randy Fine wrote : “We need more Islamophobia, not less. Fear of Islam is rational.”

And Alabama Senator Tommy Tuberville paired images of 9/11 with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, saying “The enemy is inside the gates.”

The common thread is the suggestion that Muslim identity itself is evidence of disloyalty or danger. It’s good to note that Abdul El-Sayed would be the first Muslim senator if he wins.

Republicans have made islamophobia a strategy by repeatedly casting Muslims as outsiders or potential enemies. But that, my friends, is a losing strategy, because in America, religious freedom cannot mean freedom for everyone except Muslims.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

articles.title: Calley Means, top RFK Jr. adviser, quits Trump administration
articles.summary: Calley Means, a senior adviser to Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and an outspoken advocate for the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement, resigned from the Trump administration Thursday, reportedly amid frustrations over delays in the MAHA food agenda. Means’s departure less than two weeks before the midterm elections comes amid…
articles.body:
Calley Means, a senior adviser to Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and an outspoken advocate for the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement, resigned from the Trump administration Thursday, reportedly amid frustrations over delays in the MAHA food agenda.

Means’s departure less than two weeks before the midterm elections comes amid growing frustration between grassroots MAHA activists and the Trump administration.

The MAHA base has been increasingly frustrated by the administration’s approach to its core policy goals — like eliminating pesticides and chemicals in the food supply, encouraging healthy eating by reducing reliance on ultraprocessed foods, and changing the nation’s vaccination policies.

The White House and HHS did not respond to a request for comment.

While there have been some smaller MAHA wins, many of the movement’s big priorities have been stymied by an administration and Congress that continue to hew to traditional GOP priorities.

“I am resigning from the White House with tremendous respect for President Trump and Bobby Kennedy,” Means wrote in a statement on the social platform X .

“They laid out a vision of combatting the entrenched, dark forces in DC that profit from Americans getting sick. More policy and cultural change has happened around these goals in the past 2 years than any time in history – and I know this movement is just getting started,” Means wrote.

Means mentioned some of the MAHA victories, like changing the food pyramid and reforming dietary guidelines, promoting psychedelic medicine , removing soda from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, and GRAS reform .

articles.title: Australia pastor case 'canary in the coal mine' for American Christian freedoms: TPUSA leader
articles.summary: Lucas Miles of Turning Point USA says he contacted the White House Faith Office urging Trump to pressure Australia over a church investigation.
articles.body: A Turning Point USA faith leader is calling on President Donald Trump to intervene after Australian lawmakers grilled a Christian church leader about his religious beliefs, including whether he influences members' marriages, hairstyles and even pet ownership. Lucas Miles, vice president of faith at Turning Point USA, told Fox News Digital he contacted the White House Faith Office and several administration officials over what he described as a politically motivated investigation into the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church. "We've reached out to the faith office, we've reached out to several members of the administration to make sure that they're aware of this," Miles said. "We're hoping to see some response and action soon." UK LAWMAKER WARNS IT’S ‘OPEN SEASON’ ON CHRISTIANS AS HE SOUNDS ALARM OVER ‘TWO-TIER JUSTICE’ The controversy intensified during an Oct. 16 parliamentary hearing examining allegations of coordinated political activity by church members during Australia's 2025 federal election. Independent MP Monique Ryan questioned the church's global leader, Bruce Hales, about whether members considered him an "elect vessel" or a direct messenger from God. She also asked whether members sought his guidance on marriage, housing, pets, clothing and facial hair. Liberal MP Ben Small objected to the questioning, calling it "patently ridiculous" and "so far off the terms of reference for this inquiry." Another lawmaker interjected that hairstyles had no bearing on electoral matters, while the committee chair allowed the questioning to continue. "When an Australian parliamentary committee tasked with investigating election matters begins interrogating a Christian leader about his theological convictions, serious questions must be asked about the purpose of the inquiry," Miles said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital. "Bruce Hales was summoned to answer questions about electoral conduct, not to defend the doctrines of the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church before the government," he added. BISHOP ROBERT BARRON: THE WAR ON CHRISTIANS IS REAL AND THE WORLD CAN NO LONGER STAY SILENT Miles argued that the line of questioning may illustrate a broader threat to religious freedom. "The troubling shift from election oversight to religious scrutiny gives every appearance of a politically motivated witch hunt," he said. Hales denied directing, funding or coordinating political campaigning during the 2025 election, maintaining that church members acted independently. "I had no involvement whatsoever in relation to any members who volunteered or took part in any aspect of the 2025 federal election," Hales told the committee. Lawmakers questioned whether a sermon in which Hales said Australia needed to be "happy again, smiling again" influenced members' political activities, citing subsequent campaign messaging that echoed his words. His son, Gareth, acknowledged encouraging people already involved in campaigning but denied directing an organized church campaign. CHRISTIAN WOMAN PLEADS NOT GUILTY TO NEW 'ORWELLIAN' CHARGES FOR STANDING AND SILENT PRAYER The committee is also examining allegations of intimidation and coordinated campaigning during the election. Church leaders have denied organizing or condoning improper conduct. Hales said he did not support harassment or intimidation and maintained that individual members should be accountable for their own actions. "In a free society, government has every right to investigate violations of election law, but it has no business putting Christian doctrine on trial," Miles said. The Plymouth Brethren Christian Church, which traces its roots back roughly 200 years, says its roughly 55,000 members worldwide follow a "Doctrine of Separation," distancing themselves from certain secular activities and practices they believe conflict with biblical teachings. The church rejects descriptions of the denomination as a cult, maintaining that its members freely practice their faith and contribute to their communities through businesses and charitable initiatives. The hearing also turned to the United States when Sen. Steph Hodgins-May questioned Hales about Turning Point USA's support for the church and whether church leaders had met with the Trump administration. Hales said he had never met Trump but understood that some church members in New York had briefly met the president. Miles, who is not a member of the denomination, said he wants Trump to apply diplomatic pressure on Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and urge an end to the inquiry. "What I would like to see, first of all, is some pressure applied, whether that be through diplomatic channels or through the president himself," Miles told Fox News Digital. Miles said he remains hopeful the administration will take action and warned that the controversy could establish a troubling precedent for American churches, pointing to past disputes involving religious organizations and government restrictions in the United States. "They're making this about trying to really smear the church because of specific doctrines that they might hold to, and I think this is a canary in the coal mine for religious liberty across the globe that when we see a Western nation like Australia," Miles said. "The government [is] against the church and against the Christian church in particular, I think this is reason for the rest of the world to wake up." "If this can happen in Australia, if it can happen places like England and Canada, it certainly can happen America if we don't stay alert," he said. Miles emphasized that Christians should be free to participate in politics without their churches automatically being held responsible for their individual choices. "Just because individual private citizens who happen to go to a church have a similar opinion about politics, that does not constitute a grand conspiracy," he said. He urged Trump to pursue what he called "faith-based diplomacy" to defend religious liberty abroad. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Religious liberty means nothing if it only protects those whose beliefs the government approves of," Miles said. The White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

articles.title: Sanders feuds with AIPAC over last-minute Rogers donations
articles.summary: Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) feuded online Thursday over donations from the PAC to Republican Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers. “AIPAC is now spending as much as $9 million against Abdul El-Sayed. AIPAC is why we’re at war in Iran. AIPAC is why the U.S. has supported genocide…
articles.body:
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) feuded online Thursday over donations from the PAC to Republican Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers.

“AIPAC is now spending as much as $9 million against Abdul El-Sayed. AIPAC is why we’re at war in Iran. AIPAC is why the U.S. has supported genocide in Gaza. We must say NO to AIPAC,” Sanders said in a post on the social platform X.

“YES to electing Abdul as Michigan’s next U.S. Senator,” the Vermont senator added.

AIPAC responded to Sanders with a post mocking the senator’s comments.

“AIPAC is why your fantasy football team stinks. AIPAC is why the weather is bad. AIPAC is why you need an app to park. Say NO to Bernie’s obsessive scapegoating,” AIPAC’s post said. “YES to an America that works with our ally to create U.S. jobs, keep America safe, and promote democratic values.”

El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, has expressed opposition to U.S. aid to Israel. The issue of American support for Israel has had significant prominence in U.S. politics in the past few years, especially with Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023, attacks on Israel and the war in Gaza that followed.

Many have decried Israel’s actions in Gaza as a “genocide,” with the tens of thousands of Palestinians being killed in the conflict and the territory experiencing mass infrastructure destruction and a humanitarian crisis.

The New York Times reported Wednesday that AIPAC had recently begun giving money to a super PAC backing Rogers, aiming to possibly give millions of dollars, two sources told the outlet.

articles.title: Ilhan Omar is not the Minnesota congresswoman’s 'real name': sources
articles.summary: Federal investigators say the congresswoman's real name is Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, as U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro moves to keep the warrant sealed.
articles.body: Ilhan Omar is not the "real name" of the Minnesota congresswoman, Fox News Digital has learned. Her real name is Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, according to two people familiar with the ongoing investigation into the Somali-born congresswoman, including a law enforcement source. And if proven in court that Omar has lived her "entire life under an alias," a former Minnesota federal immigration judge tells Fox News Digital that every single form she ever filled out could be "called into question." On Wednesday, U.S. District Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro filed a motion seeking to prevent the federal search warrant for the congresswoman’s home from being unsealed, which was requested by several media outlets. The motion says the federal government is not yet finished executing the search warrant, and that it shouldn’t be unsealed yet. "Before the Court are three Applications to unseal ex parte materials and proceedings related to a federal search warrant for the personal residence in the District of Columbia of Congresswoman Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar…" the motion begins. "That's not her real name," one source said when asked why the motion used the "a/k/a Ilhan Adbullahi Omar" language. Fox News Digital first reported in the midst of the search of the lawmaker's Washington, D.C. residence that federal investigators are probing whether she or her father committed fraud when filling out her immigration paperwork. Investigators obtained the elected official’s DNA and seized her personal phone and passport during the Oct. 12 pre-dawn raid. FEDERAL AGENTS SEIZE PHONE OF REP ILHAN OMAR IN RAID TIED TO IMMIGRATION FRAUD PROBE Omar’s sister, Sahra Noor, was questioned by federal investigators last week in relation to the probe, Fox News Digital exclusively reported. Conservative personality Will Chamberlain first posted the motion on X speculating that the "DOJ believes [Omar] is present in the United States under a false identity." Fox News Digital has now learned from multiple sources familiar with the investigation that Omar is not the congresswoman’s birth name. REP ILHAN OMAR'S IMMIGRATION HISTORY FACES NEW SCRUTINY AS FEDERAL INVESTIGATORS SUBPOENA RELATIVES Omar has publicly confirmed that she does not have a birth certificate. In an official U.S. House biography, her birthday is listed as Oct. 14, 1982, and states that she was born in Mogadishu, Somalia. She says she came to the U.S. with her family as refugees fleeing war-torn Somalia in 1995, when she was a minor. Omar has not been charged with a crime, and materials presented by prosecutors are only allegations. Attorneys for the embattled congresswoman did not return Fox News Digital's request for comment. Nathan Hansen, a former federal immigration judge from Minnesota, listed the extent to which the supposed name change could impact the case against the congresswoman. "You think of all the types of documents somebody like her might have filled out," he said. "There'd be federal student loan and student aid applications, maybe federal housing related applications, maybe public assistance applications, passport applications, passport information and driver's license information, Real I.D. information [and] voting information." ILHAN OMAR'S TURBULENT WEEK EXPLAINED: THE DUELING PROBES THAT THREW THE SOMALI-BORN PROGRESSIVE INTO CHAOS He said if someone has lived their entire lives under an alias, there are many criminal charges that could be levied. "Sometimes they might say that that would be a wire fraud charge, they always add that one," said Hansen. "And that's pretty broad. But, you know, a lot of these documents are sworn under penalty of perjury." "If this is not, like, a real legal name, it's got some legal backing to it that every type of government form she's filled out in her entire existence might be called into question," Hansen said. ILHAN OMAR SHOULD BE JAILED, DEPORTED IF CITIZENSHIP FRAUD PROVEN, TOP HOUSE REPUBLICAN SAYS The representative for Minnesota’s 5th Congressional District in the U.S. House, has long faced allegations that she married her brother for immigration purposes. In 2009, she legally married a man named Ahmed Nur Said Elmi. The pair split in 2017. The following year, she was elected to Congress. In 2020, she married her third husband, political consultant Tim Mynett. In Omar's first public interview since the raid on her home, she sat down with MS NOW’s Chris Hayes. During that interview, she once again denied those allegations, calling them "insane." ILHAN OMAR BELIEVES TRUMP RAID ON HOME WAS MEANT TO 'INTIMIDATE AND SCARE PEOPLE' FROM VOTING "You’re not related to him at all?" Hayes asked. "There’s not some weird kernel of truth…?" "Not to my knowledge," she replied. In the wake of the raid, Omar has accused President Donald Trump and his administration of targeting her politically. "This raid by Trump’s DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies," she said in a statement on X. HOMAN SAYS ILHAN OMAR COULD BE STRIPPED OF NATURALIZATION, DEPORTED IF IMMIGRATION FRAUD IS PROVEN "For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back," the post continued. "Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies." articles.title: Mullin on heat ray weapon: ‘We’re always evaluating technology on the border’
articles.summary: Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Wednesday that the department is “always evaluating technology on the border” after receiving a military-grade heat ray from the Pentagon. CNN reported that the heat ray — officially called the Active Denial System — emits an invisible beam of electromagnetic waves which can reach a little…
articles.body:
Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Wednesday that the department is “always evaluating technology on the border” after receiving a military-grade heat ray from the Pentagon.

CNN reported that the heat ray — officially called the Active Denial System — emits an invisible beam of electromagnetic waves which can reach a little more than half a mile away and causes a burning sensation when it comes into contact with human skin.

Pentagon officials have compared the feeling to the blast of heat when opening an oven, resulting in a 10-15 minute “tingling sensation” that generates “an instinctive and irresistible urge to run from the effect.”

“Well, listen, we’re always evaluating technology on the border,” Mullin told Fox News’s Laura Ingraham during his appearance Wednesday on “The Ingraham Angle.”

“Deterrent is the best option we have, and so any technology we can use to deter people from trying to enter this country illegally, we’re doing that.”

Mullin added that DHS will use “whatever tool we have at our disposal” to prevent migrants from illegally entering the U.S. He said he would not comment on how the technology works but said it was “less lethal or nonlethal,” and the goal is not to deploy lethal forces unless necessary.

“But that’s our goal, or goal is to say, ‘Don’t come across. … Our borders are closed. We’re not Democrats. We’re not going to allow you to come in and take advantage of the American people,'” he said.

It remains unclear how the weapon would be tested and how it might be used, with current and former Customs and Border Protection officials telling CNN there have been internal discussions at DHS about crowd dispersal along the border with Mexico.

A Defense Department official told the outlet that DHS can make an additional request to use the heat ray weapon after its seven-month loan period.

The weapon, developed by Raytheon in Waltham, Mass., was previously deployed for active combat operations in Afghanistan in 2010 but was never used.

The Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department said that same year it deployed a smaller version of the weapon to “stop or lessen the severity of inmate assaults” at the Pitchess Detention Center in Castaic, Calif., located in the Santa Clarita Valley north of Los Angeles.

The American Civil Liberties Union at the time slammed then-Los Angeles County Sheriff Lee Baca’s announcement about the weapon and urged him not to use it. The nonprofit said the military had evidence that the weapon was “capable of inflicting not only intolerable pain, but death.”

Former DHS Secretary Kirstjen Nielsen in 2018 said the weapon would not be used amid President Trump’s warnings that “caravans” of migrants were approaching the southern border, The New York Times reported. Nielsen also told an aide that using the weapon must never be brought up again.

articles.title: Ilhan Omar says she lives 'paycheck to paycheck' as DOJ probes financial disclosures
articles.summary: Ilhan Omar claims she lives "paycheck to paycheck," despite earning $174,000 and facing scrutiny over financial disclosures tied to Tim Mynett.
articles.body: Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., described herself as a member of the "working class" who lives "paycheck to paycheck" during an interview with MS NOW host Chris Hayes on Wednesday night. "I mean, it’s, you know, working — working class, I guess, like paycheck to paycheck still," Omar said. "We’ve got four kids, and we live, I think, like a basic life. I have a Toyota Camry that’s from 2016." Omar's characterization of her finances comes despite her $174,000 annual congressional salary and scrutiny over financial disclosures that once listed assets tied to her husband as being worth as much as $30 million. The comments came during Omar’s first public appearance since Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents searched her Washington, D.C., residence on Oct. 12 as part of an investigation into possible immigration-related offenses. ILHAN OMAR BELIEVES TRUMP RAID ON HOME WAS MEANT TO 'INTIMIDATE AND SCARE PEOPLE' FROM VOTING Since the raid, the representative has used the investigation twice as a reason to publicly fundraise. "That goes a long way as we fight Trump and his administration for trying to intimidate me and so many people right before the midterm elections," Omar said in a video she uploaded to social media on Wednesday. "We know that they’re running scared. We’re not going to be intimidated. We’re not going to be silenced." The Democratic National Committee has also sent out its own fundraising email based on Omar’s campaign request for money. "It’s Ilhan Omar — Trump’s DHS agents just carried out a raid and search of my home," the email says. "This is a drastic escalation of the ludicrous, partisan investigation that they launched into my immigration status." ILHAN OMAR'S WEALTH SCANDAL TAKES A TURN JUST ONE DAY AFTER RAID OF HER DC HOME Omar also acknowledged during the MS NOW interview that the federal agents who searched her home were "polite" and left the property in good condition, even folding some of her clothes. "When they left, what did you do?" Hayes asked Omar. "I just went back around the house just trying to make sure everything was put back," Omar replied. "And they did a really good job in putting everything back in its place. They actually even folded some of my clothing that [was] not folded. So it was … a very bizarre [situation]." The Minnesota Democrat added that she thought the HSI agents who raided her home were "intrusive, but polite." "And yeah, they, they left the house, I think, you know, in good shape," she told MS NOW. Omar claimed during the interview that the federal agents were searching her house for four to five hours. She added that they left the raid with more than a dozen items, including notebooks and a children’s Somali-language phrasebook. "[That] was why I was surprised when they handed me the receipt for the items that they take in, to do that long of a search and to walk away with 17 items, of like 10 that were just notebooks and, like, old phones. Was such a bizarre, bizarre thing," Omar said. A separate Justice Department investigation is examining Omar’s financial disclosures, U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said during an appearance on Fox News’ "America Reports." The disclosures previously showed that the reported value of two businesses tied to Omar’s husband, Tim Mynett, rose from as much as $51,000 in 2023 to as much as $30 million in 2024, according to House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer, R-Ky. Omar later amended the filing, saying the original figures were the result of an accounting error. The amended disclosure listed the couple’s assets at between $18,004 and $95,000. Omar has denied wrongdoing, and no criminal charges have been filed against her in connection with the disclosures. Mynett’s businesses include eStCru, a winery, and Rose Lake Capital, an investment firm. The winery has reportedly shut down. ILHAN OMAR RAID SPARKS OMINOUS PREDICTION FROM WATCHDOG: 'THEY PROBABLY GOT THE GOODS' On Fox News’ "Sunday Night in America," Comer told host Trey Gowdy that his committee’s initial review of Omar’s disclosures identified multiple issues that could justify further investigative steps. "First of all, not only was there a huge discrepancy in the financial disclosure form, there was the winery that was the big base of her $25 million listing on her financial disclosure form," Comer said. "That winery has, according to the press, been shut down because of fraud." In a February letter to Mynett, Comer noted that Omar’s 2023 disclosure listed her stake in eStCru as being worth between $15,001 and $50,000. "The following year, her financial disclosure form listed a stake in eStCru ‘worth between $1,000,001 and $5,000,000,’" Comer wrote. "There are serious public concerns about how your businesses increased so dramatically in value only a year after reporting very limited assets." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP A rank-and-file House member’s annual salary is $174,000. Members may also participate in the federal Thrift Savings Plan and qualify for a pension under the Federal Employees Retirement System, though eligibility and benefit amounts depend on factors including age, years of service and salary history. The financial investigation remains ongoing.

articles.title: Supreme Court justice turns on her own court with dire warning about American democracy
articles.summary: Elena Kagan argued the Supreme Court's gerrymandering and campaign finance rulings are destabilizing democracy and driving political polarization.
articles.body: Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan made the case that recent rulings from the conservative-majority high court are destabilizing democracy, suggesting that it isn't working "as well as it should." The remarks from the liberal justice came during a closed discussion before faculty and students at Catholic University's law school in Washington, D.C. The discussion between Kagan and law professor Joel Alicea Alicia, who previously clerked for Justice Samuel Alito, comes just weeks after the Supreme Court began its new term, during which it's expected to rule in major cases that will determine the scope of gun rights and state election integrity laws, among other issues. The conversation also comes less than two weeks before the midterm elections as President Donald Trump and Republican state lawmakers have pushed for new congressional maps drawn to favor Republicans and bolster their chances of maintaining control of the House. Democratic-led states have responded by redrawing their own maps, fueling ongoing lawsuits and court battles. SUPREME COURT KICKS OFF NEW TERM WITH FRESH QUESTIONS OVER ITS LEGITIMACY AND ITS FUTURE Kagan pointed to the Supreme Court’s 2019 ruling in Rucho v. Common Cause, in which she dissented, as the beginning of a "race to the bottom." She argued that the decision, which barred federal courts from invalidating maps solely because they unfairly favor one political party, deprived "masses of citizens" of their "rights to voting equality." Kagan suggested that the influx of gerrymandered maps is "driving people away from the center toward the wings, toward the extremes. "Making what I think is, unfortunately, a too polarized country even more so," Kagan said. Kagan also criticized rulings from the previous term, including the court’s decision limiting campaign finance restrictions and its ruling that made it more difficult to draw majority-minority congressional districts under the Voting Rights Act. "Part of the reason why the court got it wrong was a kind of lack of the appropriate concern or understanding of the consequences of their decisions," Kagan said. "I do think in all these areas the court has blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political system works and has created a democracy that doesn’t work as well as it should." DESANTIS SIGNS FLORIDA REDISTRICTING MAP TO POTENTIALLY FLIP 4 HOUSE SEATS RED Last term, the Supreme Court struck down federal limits on how much state and national political parties could spend in coordination with their candidates. Meanwhile, Kagan argued in dissent that the limits were necessary to prevent wealthy donors from working around direct contribution caps and that striking them down effectively allowed a political party to become an "alternative checking account" for a candidate. "The people of America look around this political system and think that all this money chasing all these political candidates is a nightmare," Kagan said. "And they’re right." Kagan, who was appointed to the court by President Barack Obama in 2010, argued that it was in a much better position when there was greater ideological balance. "There was a period of time where the court was in a better place, and the country was in a better place because the court was more balanced, and it was unclear whether the court could push through anybody’s program." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "Nobody in America thought that the court was in the pocket of any one group or any one party," she said. "And the court had a kind of legitimacy. When the court has a legitimacy of that kind, it helps to create a stable country." However, Kagan pushed back against the characterization that the conservative-leaning court simply rubber-stamped Trump's entire agenda. She pointed to previous rulings by the high court rejecting birthright citizenship restrictions, tariffs and Trump's restrictions on mail-in voting. articles.title: Trump doubles down on anti-Acton ad in Ohio: ‘Vivek should keep it up’
articles.summary: President Trump defended Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s ad featuring his Democratic opponent Amy Acton’s estranged mother on Thursday, saying the Republican “should keep it up.” In a lengthy Truth Social post, Trump hit Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R) over his calls for Ramaswamy to take down the ad earlier Thursday. In the video, Acton’s mother…
articles.body:
President Trump defended Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s ad featuring his Democratic opponent Amy Acton’s estranged mother on Thursday, saying the Republican “should keep it up.”

In a lengthy Truth Social post , Trump hit Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R) over his calls for Ramaswamy to take down the ad earlier Thursday. In the video, Acton’s mother suggests her daughter has mental health issues.

“Our RINO Governor of Ohio, Mike DeWine, who I unfortunately helped get elected years ago, when he was losing by 16 points prior to my doing a Rally for him was, as usual, disloyal to the Republican Party,” Trump wrote.

“He strongly suggested that Vivek should, ‘take down the Ad.’ He probably wants a Dumocrat to win, and certainly doesn’t want someone who will do a much better job than he is capable of doing. I suggested, on the other hand, that Vivek should keep it up,” he continued.

Acton’s brother released a statement after the ad aired stating that he and his sister have been estranged from their mother since Acton was 12 because their mother stayed married to the man who sexually abused Acton at a young age.

Trump’s comments come as many Ohio Republicans have condemned the ad . Sen. Jon Husted (R), who is facing a tough reelection bid in the state, has sought to distance himself from the ad. The incumbent senator said in a statement to The Associated Press on Wednesday that he would not have run the ad.

Trump, meanwhile, defended Acton’s mother in the Thursday social media post, saying she was courageous for participating in the ad.

“That took a lot of courage to do but, essentially, what she was really doing was saving Ohio from making a truly horrible choice! The Press is trying to convince everyone that this Ad is bad, because it’s so good! Who wouldn’t use such an Ad? I would, it’s called, ‘hitting pay dirt,’” the president said. “The fact is, Lyin’ Amy Acton, who I’ve never even heard of before, has been lying about Vivek for the entire Campaign.”

Trump’s comments on the matter are similar to those from Vice President Vance, who told reporters on Wednesday that he was “disgusted” by the Republican criticism of the ad.

“I have to admit that I’m a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America,” Vance told reporters.

articles.title: Supreme Court Justice Kagan warns some conservative rulings have been 'destructive of our democracy'
articles.summary: Justice Elena Kagan warned that Supreme Court rulings on gerrymandering and campaign finance have created a democracy that "doesn't work" for everyone.
articles.body: Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan suggested Tuesday that some recent decisions by her conservative colleagues have undermined democracy, while admitting at times they had also pushed back against the Trump administration. Kagan took part in a discussion on recent U.S. Supreme Court decisions while speaking at Catholic University's Columbus School of Law. She specifically took issue with cases like Louisiana v. Callais, which ruled in a 6-3 decision that race-based gerrymandering of congressional districts was unconstitutional. In her dissent, Kagan called the decision the "latest chapter in the majority's now-completed demolition of the Voting Rights Act" and she continued to criticize election and campaign finance decisions made by the court. KAMALA HARRIS CALLS TO EXPAND SUPREME COURT, ADD STATES IF DEMS TAKE CONGRESS "Part of the reason why the court got it wrong was a kind of lack of the appropriate concern or understanding of the consequences of their decisions," Kagan said, according to NBC News. She went on to warn that decisions that undermined voters' ability to choose their candidates were "very destructive of our democracy." "I do think in all these areas the court has blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political system works and has created a democracy that doesn't work as well as it should," Kagan said. SUPREME COURT CHIEF JUSTICE PINPOINTS WHAT AMERICANS MISUNDERSTAND ABOUT HIM AND HIS COLLEAGUES She also criticized the conservative view of originalism in the Supreme Court, calling it "misconceived" and "not a very good match with the Constitution we have." Kagan claimed that these and other decisions have contributed to the country becoming more "polarized," particularly around campaign finance. "I think you know the people of America look around this political system and think that all this money, chasing all these political candidates, is a nightmare, and they're right," she said. CONSERVATIVE GROUPS SAY JUSTICE KAGAN CANNOT BE IMPARTIAL IN UPCOMING SUPREME COURT CLIMATE LITIGATION However, Kagan stopped short of accusing the court of being beholden to President Donald Trump, pointing out several cases where even conservative justices "definitely pushed back" on his agenda. Trump nominated three of the current justices on the court in Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett. In a comment to Fox News Digital, Heritage Foundation Senior Legal Fellow of Courts and the Constitution Zack Smith denounced Kagan and what he characterized as far-left politicians' efforts to delegitimize SCOTUS decisions. "The job of the Court is not to play politics with its decisions. Instead, its job is to faithfully apply the Constitution and other laws as they are written. Justice Kagan has disagreed with the majority of her colleagues in some of those decisions, but that doesn't mean they are illegitimate or even wrongly decided," Smith said. articles.title: Trump laments NYC horse-drawn carriage ban
articles.summary: President Trump said Thursday he is sad to see the horse-drawn carriages in New York City go as the New York City Council is expected to pass a ban on them. The council is expected to vote on the decision Thursday, and the ban would start in 2028. “So sad to see the beloved Central…
articles.body:
President Trump said Thursday he is sad to see the horse-drawn carriages in New York City go as the New York City Council is expected to pass a ban on them.

The council is expected to vote on the decision Thursday, and the ban would start in 2028.

“So sad to see the beloved Central Park Horse-drawn Carriage Industry ending after over a Century, based largely on one tragic accident,” he wrote on Truth Social. “When there is a car accident in the area, of which there are many, they don’t stop cars from entering the Park.”

“So why would they stop the Carriages? It was a Great Tradition,” he said. “Another piece of History that’s gone. It will be missed!”

In a second post, he said, “The Horse-drawn Carriage in New York City is a quintessential New York experience. So sad that, for political reasons, we will see it go!”

Horse-drawn carriages have been in New York City for more than 150 years.

Romanch Mahajan, an 18-year-old tourist, died last year after he got off the carriage as the horse sprinted through the park without its driver.

The law the council is voting on is called Romanch’s Law after the young tourist.

There have been attempts for years to shut down the industry, with some saying it’s inhumane for the horses.

“The horse carriage industry is coming to an end in New York City,” New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) said. “Our administration will make sure workers and owners are protected and the horses are safe.”

The legislation would require Mamdani’s office to come up with a plan by April to help the remaining carriage drivers find other work, according to reports.

articles.title: State Department asked some career diplomats about voting for Trump: Report
articles.summary: The State Department is asking some career diplomats who are applying for senior assignments about their voting history in the past three presidential elections, according to a report. Candidates who voted for President Trump would be eligible for the mid- to upper-level foreign service roles, the Washington Sun reported, adding that campaign donations were also…
articles.body:
The State Department is asking some career diplomats who are applying for senior assignments about their voting history in the past three presidential elections, according to a report.

Candidates who voted for President Trump would be eligible for the mid- to upper-level foreign service roles, the Washington Sun reported , adding that campaign donations were also scrutinized.

Federal law directly prohibits federal officials from discriminating against staff based on political affiliation.

A State Department spokesperson rejected “this absurd premise” that people are being asked about political affiliation, including for promotions.

“As it has been expressed repeatedly, this Administration will prioritize merit rather than giving out leadership positions based on the number of years individuals have been at the Department,” the spokesperson told The Hill on Thursday.

The spokesperson added that questions to foreign service and civil service officers surrounding “fidelity” mean upholding the Constitution and law, and executing policy “with loyalty to the American people and their interests.”

“It is not about partisan behavior but rather about executing the President’s vision for foreign policy.”

The American Foreign Service Association (AFSA), the professional association and union for foreign service officers, has heard anecdotes of senior foreign service members not getting jobs after going through interviews with questions that were political in nature.

The AFSA said such questioning has no place in the federal service and is exploring legal options.

Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), the outgoing ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said the committee has been following “for some time now” whether the Trump administration is making political affiliation a factor in employment.

“These are critical national security positions and individuals should be chosen for their experience and ability, not their political loyalty. We are working with the House and other relevant committees to thoroughly investigate all such claims,” Shaheen told the Sun.

Likewise, Rep. James Walkinshaw (D-Va.), a member of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, raised concern about the Sun’s reporting.

“Making civil service decisions based on political affiliations or donations is flat out illegal and anyone involved in implementing this should know that they will be held accountable,” he wrote on the social platform X .

Rubio’s State Department added evaluating a career officer’s “fidelity” as part of criterion that looks at how an employee protects and promotes executive power starting in July 2025, Federal News Network reported at the time . The fidelity portion of the scorecard links to a White House webpage listing Trump’s executive orders and presidential actions, it reported.

Career foreign and civil service officers in the State Department are required by federal law to carry out their duties in a neutral and nonpartisan manner. These professionals hold the majority of positions in the agency, while the executive branch retains the right to put in place political appointees.

Democrats have criticized the Trump administration’s reorganization at the State Department as pushing out nonpartisan career staff and filling ranks with political appointees, shrinking the opportunities for career staff to advance their careers.

Earlier this year, Rubio laid off approximately 1,100 civil service and 250 foreign service officers as part of what the department described as a “reorganization effort.”

Rubio defended the layoffs at the time as the result of eliminating specific bureaus and offices as part of the reorganization. But critics said staff trained to be generalists and moved around were unfairly and cynically eliminated by virtue of being in the wrong office at the wrong time.

A shrinking list of opportunities for high-level roles has also led to a surge in retirements among senior career staff, NPR reported earlier this year , as political appointees have increasingly filled ambassadorships and other posts have remained empty.

Democrats have denounced the Trump administration’s reorganization efforts as pushing out professional staff with decades of experience in critical foreign policy areas in favor of political loyalists. They point to the Trump administration’s abrupt elimination of the U.S. Agency for International Development and its 16,000 staff as dismissing foreign policy expertise for political aims.

Former State Department officials who served in both Republican and Democratic administrations pointed to the Sun’s reporting as another example of the Trump administration’s increased politicization across the federal government.

“No surprise. Just confirmation that State – like DOJ [Department of Justice] – has become an instrument of Administration politics goals/preferences,” Aaron David Miller, a veteran diplomat focused on the Middle East in both Democratic and Republican administrations, posted on X .

Daniel Fried, a former ambassador to Poland, called partisanship testing as a criteria for promotion “(a) dumb and (b) illegal,” in a post on X .

Likewise, Luis Moreno, a former ambassador and member of the American Academy of Diplomacy, criticized the move as elevating “political hacks” over professionals.

“I came into the Foreign Service under Ronald Reagan, served under every president, even a few months under Donald Trump. NO ONE, absolutely NO ONE, ever asked me who I voted for or doubted my “fidelity” to my country. They don’t want professionals, they want political hacks,” he posted on X .

articles.title: Carville says he still believes Trump will quit by Easter
articles.summary: Democratic strategist James Carville doubled down Wednesday on his prediction that President Trump will leave office by Easter next year. Fox News’s Laura Ingraham asked Carville during an interview on “The Ingraham Angle” if he stuck by the prediction he made earlier this year and why. Carville said he does, adding that Trump’s “not particularly…
articles.body:
Democratic strategist James Carville doubled down Wednesday on his prediction that President Trump will leave office by Easter next year.

Fox News’s Laura Ingraham asked Carville during an interview on “The Ingraham Angle” if he stuck by the prediction he made earlier this year and why. Carville said he does, adding that Trump’s “not particularly a hard man.”

“And when he sees what’s going to happen in this election, and I had this hit me in 1994, I know what this is. Most people don’t. And when these things hit, of course, [former President] Clinton was able to survive because he was young, he was brilliant, and he had Newt Gingrich as his foil,” he said, referring to the former Republican House Speaker from Georgia.

“Do you want to put some money on this, Carville?” Ingraham asked. “I will put a huge amount on this, that Trump will be out by Easter, for charity.”

Carville poured cold water on the offer, saying he does not “do the predictable thing.”

“I like to think of the future,” he said. “I think he’s going to get really bored and when you lose one this big, people don’t really pay attention to you.”

Carville predicted on his “ Politics War Room ” podcast in June that Trump — whom he said was “soft,” “distracted” and “bored with the Iran war” — would leave if Democrats make “breathtaking” victories in the November midterm elections.

“He’s obviously not well, he sleeps all the time, slobbers all over himself or whatever,” Carville said at the time.

He added that Trump will be responding to the “massive rejection of him, anybody that has anything to do with him, anything that has anything to do with [him].”

Carville reiterated his prognostication , saying Trump’s “just going to f—ing walk away,” unable to come to grips with “a massive rejection of him.”

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle, in a statement to The Hill at the time, called Carville “a stone-cold loser who suffers from a severe and incurable disease known as Trump Derangement Syndrome, and it has rotted his peanut-sized brain.”

Carville has also since claimed he “has” Trump Derangement Syndrome, saying Monday that if he “could take a pill that would help me hate that motherf‑‑‑er more and obsess on him more, I would take that pill.”

Democrats appear to be poised to reclaim the House and potentially the Senate in next month’s midterms, dealing significant blows to Trump. The Hill’s election partner Decision Desk HQ forecasts a 78 percent probability they will win back the House in November, and a 57 percent probability Democrats could reclaim the Senate from Republicans.

articles.title: Acton fundraising surges following controversial ad
articles.summary: Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton (D) has seen a surge in donations after she was the target of a controversial attack ad from her Republican opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy. Acton surged into second place on Democratic political fundraising site ActBlue’s “trending campaigns,” only behind James Talarico, the Texas Democrat running for Senate. Ramaswamy’s ad sparked bipartisan…
articles.body:
Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton (D) has seen a surge in donations after she was the target of a controversial attack ad from her Republican opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy.

Acton surged into second place on Democratic political fundraising site ActBlue’s “trending campaigns,” only behind James Talarico, the Texas Democrat running for Senate.

Ramaswamy’s ad sparked bipartisan backlash for featuring his opponent’s estranged mother, who called her daughter a “liar” and warned voters not to support her election bid. The Democrat’s campaign responded, sharing she had been sexually abused by her stepfather at a young age, and her mother stayed with him until his death. Acton was removed from her mother’s custody at age 12.

In an email to supporters following the ad’s release, Acton said she needs more funds to counter Ramaswamy’s spending advantage.

“We need to send a clear message: this kind of hate and vitriol has no place in Ohio,” Acton said in a fundraising email. “But I’ll be frank – we’re still being outspent by a large margin, and if we allow him to dominate the airwaves for these final 12 days, we’ll be at a real disadvantage on Election Day.”

In addition to fundraising from supporters, Illinois first lady MK Pritzker, the wife of billionaire Gov. JB Pritzker (D), announced a $500,000 donation to Acton’s campaign in response to the ad, saying “Ohio deserves better” than Ramaswamy.

Acton’s fundraising email bashed the Ohio Republican and former presidential candidate for his tactics.

“Vivek Ramaswamy has unleashed attack ads against me that have gone too far,” the Democrat said. “He’s stooped so low that even Republicans are calling him out. He’s showing Ohio exactly who he is: a man willing to go to despicable lows to win.”

The personal nature of the ad drew criticism and condemnation from both parties, including from Ohio’s current GOP governor, Mike DeWine, who said the “deeply troubling” ad should be pulled from the air.

Still, both President Trump and Vice President Vance defended Ramaswamy, with Vance saying he was “disgusted” by Republicans who pushed back on the ad. Trump attacked DeWine for criticizing the ad in a Truth Social post Thursday, telling the GOP candidate to “keep it up.”

The Buckeye State’s highly competitive gubernatorial contest is one of the most expensive in the country.

Acton has outraised Ramaswamy, but the Republican is supported by millions in outside spending. As of early October, GOP-aligned groups have spent more than $100 million on ads for the race, compared with just $40 million for groups supporting Democrats, according to advertising intelligence platform AdImpact.

Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, gives Acton a 61 percent chance of defeating Ramaswamy in November.

articles.title: Epstein, Iran and ‘drain the swamp’: Have Republicans shifted before vote?
articles.summary: Some of the core issues that drove Trump’s US supporters and the MAGA movement are no longer Republican talking points.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has long touted himself as a political outsider, someone who would expose the elites’ abuse of power and shift government focus from far-off conflicts to problems at home. Phrases like “drain the swamp” and “America first” have proved to be powerful rallying cries, sparking a whole cadre of “Make America Great Again” (MAGA) Republicans.

Halfway through his final term as president, though, Trump has backpedalled on many of those ideas, cosying up to the ultra-wealthy, sidelining investigations into convicted sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein, and launching an ongoing war with Iran.

That about-face appears to be having a real impact on Republicans running in the US midterm elections in November, said Rina Shah, a geopolitical adviser and strategist and a former senior GOP congressional aide.

“In competitive races, some are quietly distancing,” Shah said, adding that they are “talking about gas prices, local issues, or [saying] ‘I’m focused on my district’ – because the Iran war and the Epstein drip are already showing up in attack ads and soft polling.”

Here’s what you need to know about whether the Republican Party has softened its stance on these issues.

Which Republicans have broken with Trump over the Epstein files?

During his 2024 presidential campaign, Trump said he would declassify troves of files kept by the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) about Epstein and his global network of contacts. Trump’s future cabinet members, too, were enthusiastic about this, with Kash Patel, now head of the FBI, saying it was time to “put on your big boy pants and let us know who the pedophiles are”.

Yet a few months after taking office, Trump began dragging his feet, sparking a backlash from influential MAGA figures. Trump began calling the entire issue a “hoax” and saying Republicans were being duped by Democrats into calling for an investigation into Epstein’s network.

Congress did eventually force the release of the files, with help from a handful of Republicans who broke with Trump. The Trump administration has released batches of the heavily redacted files, but has continued to withhold some. Meanwhile, all the Republican lawmakers who voted to mandate releases have paid a price for their insubordination, with three even losing their offices.

US Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene left her Georgia seat in January 2026, after publicly clashing with Trump over Epstein. Nancy Mace, a Republican from South Carolina, lost her bid to become the party’s candidate in her home state after Trump refused to endorse her. Colorado’s Lauren Boebert barely won the primary in her own contest after angering Trump by supporting calls for transparency from Thomas Massie, another Republican bent on exposing what the files held. Massie, of Kentucky, also drew Trump’s ire, which likely cost him the primary.

Trump had long said he would be reducing foreign military involvement, breaking with the interventionist tendencies of other recent Republican presidents. Now he and his party face tough questions about the US-Israel war on Iran, which influential figures in the MAGA movement like political commentator Tucker Carlson have called a mistake , saying, “This is Israel’s war. This is not the United States’ war.”

Amongst disgruntled MAGA supporters, a narrative has emerged of Trump using the war to also distract from the Epstein issue. Massie, the former congressman, summed up the sentiment by saying, “Bombing a country on the other side of the globe won’t make the Epstein files go away.”

Trump has tried to downplay the war’s impact, but voters, even in the Republican Party, think he broke his own promise, driving the overall approval rating for the ratings-obsessed president down to record lows. “Seven months into an open-ended campaign with shifting goals,” said Shah, “that promise looks different to a lot of his voters.”

Few Republicans, however, have responded to that public sentiment with their votes in Congress, where Democrats have tried repeatedly to curtail Trump’s war on Iran by passing resolutions pointing out he failed to get the body’s approval.

In September, just seven Republican House members joined Democrats to pass an anti-war bill. In the Senate, similar efforts have been supported by just a handful of Republicans. Trump called the Republican lawmakers supporting the anti-war bills “unpatriotic,” and said, “They should be ashamed of themselves.”

As with the Epstein files, Trump took action against rebellious Republicans over the Iran war, for instance backing a rival of Senator Bill Cassidy, who voted in favour of the anti-war bill, in a primary in Louisiana that the Republican senator ended up losing.

What happened to Trump’s promise to ‘drain the swamp’?

One of Trump’s most appealing promises had been to purge the government of a “deep state” establishment he says is running the country without being accountable to the public on social issues, and fiscal and foreign policy.

In a way, Trump did keep that promise. An entire federal government division – the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) – forced tens of thousands of federal workers out of their jobs and dismantled institutions like the US Agency for International Development ( USAID ). The military threw out notions of racial, gender, and economic diversity. Everything from universities to the Smithsonian Institution was subjected to a campaign against an unqualified, diversity-obsessed elitist class.

But lobbying groups, including some supporting foreign governments , have been given a free hand, and ethics rules and watchdogs who would tackle political corruption have been weakened, said Shah, the Republican strategist.

At his presidential inauguration , Trump literally surrounded himself with the wealthiest people in the world, some of whom have gone on to play some part in his administration.

articles.title: Trump attacks Ohio governor over call for Ramaswamy to drop ‘deeply troubling’ ad
articles.summary: Republican Mike DeWine said ad featuring estranged mother of Democrat Amy Acton was ‘wrong’
articles.body:
Donald Trump issued a swift rebuke against Mike DeWine, Ohio's Republican governor, who on Thursday said gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy was "wrong" to release an ad critical of his Democratic rival Amy Acton that featured her estranged mother.

DeWine had implored Ramaswamy to take the ad down, but hours later, Trump urged Ramaswamy to keep airing it and accused the Republican governor of disloyalty.

Acton, who has led the Republican nominee Ramaswamy in recent polls of the governor's race, has said she has not seen her mother Donna Arthur for decades, after her mother married a man who sexually abused Acton when she was 12 years old and stayed with him even after police stepped in.

Calling the ad "deeply, deeply troubling", DeWine told reporters at the Ohio state capital. "It's wrong to run this ad," the Associated Press reported .

"I would just urge the Ramaswamy campaign to take this down," the governor added.

The video, which began circulating on social media earlier this week and which Ramaswamy's campaign later told Ohio media outlets is their work, shows Arthur calling her daughter "a liar" and saying she should not be put in charge of the state. Ramaswamy's campaign said later in the week it would spend $4m to air the ad across the state.

DeWine noted that "family members have always historically been off limits" and Acton had earlier this year mentioned Ramaswamy's mother's involvement in an alleged "pump and dump" scheme, though with less prominence than the Ramaswamy ad.

On Truth Social Thursday afternoon, Trump excoriated DeWine for his comments, saying DeWine was "disloyal to the Republican party".

"He probably wants a Dumocrat to win, and certainly doesn't want someone who will do a much better job than he is capable of doing," Trump wrote. "I suggested, on the other hand, that Vivek should keep it up, and let everyone listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest, and incapable Candidate, explain how the daughter is a DISASTER who, uncontrollably, lies, cheats, and steals!"

Connie Luck, a spokesperson for the Republican's campaign, said: "We refuse to accept the media's double standards when Democrats have regularly used family members of President Trump, RFK Jr, and other Republicans in ads. Voters shouldn't buy it."

Speaking to reporters in Cincinnati on Wednesday, Vice-President JD Vance dismissed criticism of Ramaswamy's campaign. "Whether the ad was appropriate or not is not really my concern," Vance said.

"I'm a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America. Politics is a tough business."

In a statement released by Acton's campaign, her brother, Philip Stearns, called the ad "a despicable low" for Ramaswamy, and noted that he and his sister were removed from Arthur's custody after her stepfather was arrested.

The Republican US senator Jon Husted, who is facing a election bid that could decide which party controls the chamber in the 3 November midterm elections, joined in the condemnation. "I would not have run that ad," he told the Associated Press.

His Democratic opponent, former senator Sherrod Brown, has called the video "disgusting", and said all candidates should denounce it.

Ohio's Republican secretary of state, Frank LaRose, also criticized Ramaswamy, telling the Columbus-area broadcaster ABC 6 : "I probably wouldn't run an ad like that, but every candidate gets to make their own decision."

DeWine nonetheless declined to drop his endorsement of Ramaswamy in the governor's race, saying he wanted to support the "full ticket" of Republican candidates in the midterms.

articles.title: Trump World ups attacks on Politico despite correction on Wiles story
articles.summary: Trump administration officials and allies reupped criticism of Politico this week after the news outlet issued a correction on a story about White House chief of staff Susie Wiles. Politico updated their reporting Wednesday to note that the piece incorrectly stated Wiles played a direct role in setting up ousted press secretary Katie Zacharia’s viral…
articles.body:
Trump administration officials and allies reupped criticism of Politico this week after the news outlet issued a correction on a story about White House chief of staff Susie Wiles.

Politico updated their reporting Wednesday to note that the piece incorrectly stated Wiles played a direct role in setting up ousted press secretary Katie Zacharia’s viral interview with Sean Hannity after Fox News and the White House both disputed this characterization.

A senior White House official clarified to the outlet that Wiles only “offered positive reinforcement” for this booking. In a social media post linking to the updated article, Politico noted the original story “mischaracterized Wiles’ role in connection with this interview.”

“Let me get this straight -@politico published a false story saying the exact opposite of what this now-released story says and their explanatory note says they ‘mischaracterized’ the events?” Scott Kupor, director of the U.S. Office of Personnel Management, wrote on social media Thursday in response. “I don’t think that word ‘mischaracterized’ means what you think it means!”

Former press secretary Karoline Leavitt also slammed Politico in a social media post , labeling them as “the worst outlet in Washington” following their correction.

“They constantly peddle false gossip and malicious lies from clueless anonymous sources to demean the Trump Administration,” she wrote.

“Much of my time as Press Secretary was spent disproving and killing fake stories they were adamant about writing,” Leavitt continued. “They may have issued a correction on this one, but the damage has already been done. 100% Fake News.”

After Leavitt’s departure from her role in August, the Trump administration barred Politico, CNN and MS NOW from accessing the White House over disputes with their coverage of President Trump. Journalists from these outlets eventually had their press credentials restored after a federal judge ruled against the administration’s decision.

Conservative podcaster Katie Miller, wife of Trump adviser Stephen Miller, pointed to Politico’s Berlin-based parent company Axel Springer SE as evidence the outlet was producing “anti-American fake news pushed by foreign influences.”

GOP strategists Alex Bruesewitz and Danielle Alvarez similarly criticized the outlet over this error in social media posts.

Alvarez, who served as a senior adviser on Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, said Politico “should be embarrassed.”

“Politico’s reckless disregard for the truth is a disgrace to journalism,” she wrote on social media Thursday. “At this point, the question isn’t whether Politico got the facts wrong — it’s why its editors continue to publish claims they know are false.”
